memory_candidates.content: When migrating a shell script from `set -uo pipefail` to `set -euo pipefail`, a `VAR=$(cmd); status=$?` pair immediately after is an -e-hostile pattern: under -e, a failing bare assignment aborts the script on that line, before the status capture or any custom error handling can run. Fix with `if VAR=$(cmd); then status=0; else status=$?; fi` (equivalently `VAR=$(cmd) || status=$?`) -- both forms make the assignment part of a tested condition, which is -e-exempt, and preserve the captured status exactly. This pattern recurred across two batches of one script-hygiene migration (12+ occurrences across state-write.sh, task-lock.sh, git-commit-scoped.sh, orchestrate-batch-admit.sh, orchestrate-predispatch-review.sh, orchestrate-dry-run-report.sh, orchestrate-recover-outcome.sh, and orchestrate-triage-classify.sh) -- treat it as a near-certain finding whenever a script pairs a bare `VAR=$(cmd)` with a `status=$?`/`exit=$?` on the very next line, and grep broadly for bare `=$?` (not just `status=$?`) since the captured variable name varies.

A second, easy-to-miss -e-hostile bash pattern distinct from the VAR=$(cmd); status=$? anti-pattern: a bare standalone statement of the form `[ cond ] && action` (e.g. `[ -n "$x" ] && echo ... >&2`, `[ cond ] && continue`, `[ "$FLAG" = true ] && return 0`). Under `set -e` this aborts the script whenever the CONDITION is false, not just when `action` itself fails -- because a standalone `test && cmd` statement's own exit status is the test's exit status when the test is false and `cmd` never runs. This is easy to miss during an -e migration audit because it looks like ordinary short-circuit idiom. Several instances found across a 27-file migration sat directly on a SUCCESS path rather than a failure path (e.g. `[ -z "$session_id" ] && exit_success` aborted precisely when a marker WAS found with a valid session_id -- the normal case a hook exists to handle) -- an audit that only reasons about 'what happens on failure' misses this class; the correct question is 'what happens on every branch this statement can take'. Fix: append `|| true`, or restructure as an explicit `if`. Search with `grep -n '\[ .* \] &&[^&]*$' <file> | grep -v '||'`.

When auditing a shell script for set -e migration hazards, guard a heavily-reused leaf helper FUNCTION at its own definition rather than guarding every individual call site. `deploy-root-guard.sh`-style scripts that refuse to run outside a deployed .claude/scripts/ tree can still be live-fixture-tested without touching the real deployed tree -- build an isolated `mktemp -d` fixture shaped like `$WORK/.claude/scripts/` (copy the script under test plus its lib/*.sh and deploy-root-guard.sh dependencies there, with `$WORK/specs/` two levels up) and exercise every subcommand/exit-code path against it. Two further hazard classes recur beyond the two anti-patterns above: (1) bare grep/jq command-substitution captures whose common case IS the no-match/failure path -- e.g. a PreToolUse hook's `ADD_SEGMENTS=$(echo "$CMD" | grep -oE 'git add...')` fails under pipefail on every command that ISN'T a git-add, i.e. almost every real invocation; (2) a standalone `((VAR++))` post-increment command fails under -e whenever the pre-increment value is 0 (virtually always on a loop's first iteration) -- fix by rewriting as `VAR=$((VAR + 1))`, a plain assignment immune to this hazard. For a `set -e`-fixed hook with a documented fail-open contract on internal error (e.g. 'fails OPEN if its own shared pattern library cannot be sourced'), check whether that contract was only ever honored for a MISSING dependency, not a present-but-broken one -- a `. "$LIB"` sourcing failure needs its own explicit `if ! . "$LIB"; then ... exit 0; fi` guard to honor the same contract under -e.
